title: Sebastian (20 January)
hook: a soldier-martyr painted pierced with arrows, who in his story survives them; patron of athletes

segments.voice: Yesterday, Anthony the Abbot, who heard one Gospel line and walked into the desert. Your line was the father of monks. What kindness did an animal get from you? Day nine hundred fifty-nine.

In a gallery of old paintings, a young man looks back at you, tied to a tree or a column, calm, with arrows standing out of his body. It's easy to assume you're looking at the moment he died. In his story, they aren't. The arrows are the part he survived. His name is Sebastian, and today ends a week of saints from the calendar's first weeks of January. Today, the soldier, and what happened after the arrows.
screen: `A YOUNG MAN AND THE ARROWS.` → `NOT THE MOMENT HE DIED.` → `WHAT CAME AFTER.`

segments.voice: Very little about Sebastian is certain. Saint Ambrose, the bishop of Milan, mentions him as a martyr from Milan who died in Rome. The full story comes from a much later account of his martyrdom. Here is the story it tells, the one the Church has handed down. Sebastian was an officer in the emperor's guard and a Christian, quietly. He used his post to visit Christians in prison and to keep their courage up. When he was found out, the emperor had him tied up and shot with arrows by his own fellow soldiers, and left for dead. A Christian widow named Irene came at night to take his body for burial, and found him breathing. She took him home and nursed him. And here's the turn. Healed, Sebastian did not leave Rome. He went and stood where the emperor would pass, and told him to his face that he was wrong to persecute Christians. This time he was beaten to death. So the arrows didn't stop him. Tradition honors him as a patron of athletes and soldiers, and some readers see why: a body that took the blow and got back up. Some readers hear in him the words Paul writes near the end of his second letter to Timothy. In the Douay-Rheims: "I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith." A fight, a race, a finish line. Look back at this week's calendar and you'll see a whole team: Genevieve calming Paris, Kuriakose Chavara putting a school beside a church, André the doorkeeper, Marguerite teaching in a stable, Hilary refusing to sign, Anthony walking into the desert. And Sebastian, getting back up.
screen: `A REAL MARTYR, A LATER LEGEND.` · `A SOLDIER WHO VISITED PRISONERS.` · `IRENE FINDS HIM BREATHING.` · `HE GOES BACK TO THE EMPEROR.` · then, large: `I HAVE FINISHED MY COURSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for athletes. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who trains their body. A kid at Saturday soccer, a friend who runs before work, a player on a team you follow, someone learning to walk again after an injury. Picture them in the hard part, the last stretch, the moment they want to stop. If you pray, you can ask Sebastian to pray for them. If you don't, wish them strength and a safe body, one name at a time. The bell holds the time.
Sebastian. A soldier-martyr of Rome. In his story he survived the arrows, was nursed by Irene, and went back to face the emperor.
Your line: arrows didn't stop him. Today, when something knocks you flat, take one small step of getting back up, and notice who helped you, the way Irene helped him. Day nine hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Catholics keep Saint Sebastian's memorial in January, and sports clubs, athletes and soldiers in various places honor him as a patron.
